title: The customer who wanted to be heard
text:
The call started badly. The customer had been transferred twice, repeated his order number three times, and was now speaking very loudly.

The agent, Vesela, did something that isn't in most scripts. She stopped explaining the policy and said one sentence: "You've told this story three times already, and that's our fault, not yours."

There was a pause. Then the volume dropped.

The actual problem was small. A delayed delivery, four days late, with no update from anyone. The item was still coming. What had made him angry was silence, not the delay.

Vesela gave him the tracking number, told him honestly that Thursday was realistic and Wednesday was not, and promised to call him herself if anything changed. She wrote proper case notes so nobody would ask him to explain it again.

He stayed a customer. Two months later he ordered again and mentioned her name in the comments field.

Her manager used the recording in training, with one instruction: listen to the first thirty seconds, and notice that she solved nothing in them.

options: She acknowledged the company's failure before explaining anything
She transferred him to a manager

questions.q: What did she promise about the delivery?
options: Thursday, honestly, rather than a hopeful Wednesday

questions.q: What was the manager's point about the recording?
options: The first thirty seconds solved nothing but changed everything

title: Two questions instead of twelve
text:
The old satisfaction survey had twelve questions. Around 4% of customers completed it, and most of those were people who were either delighted or furious.

The head of service replaced it with two questions. Did we solve your problem? And what would have made this easier?

Completion rose to 31%.

The first question gave a number the team could track. The second gave something more useful. In the first month, 140 people answered it, and roughly a third wrote a version of the same sentence: they had not known their case was still open.

Nothing was wrong with the resolution time. The problem was silence between updates.

The team introduced one rule. Every open case gets a message every 48 hours, even when the message is "no change yet, still with the supplier, next update Friday."

Complaint volumes fell 22% in three months. Resolution time barely moved.

The head of service is honest about what this taught her. They had spent two years trying to be faster, when customers had mostly been asking them to be present.

questions.q: What was wrong with the old survey?
options: It was only available by phone

questions.q: What did the second question reveal?
options: Customers didn't know their case was still open

questions.q: What rule did the team introduce?
options: An update every 48 hours, even with no news

questions.q: What did the head of service conclude?
options: Customers wanted presence more than speed
Resolution time is the key metric
